title: Advancing Ultrafast Electron Microscopy with RF-Driven and Frequency Tunable Pulser
content: Ultrafast electron microscopy (UEM) has emerged as an essential tool in materials science, enabling the study of nanoscale dynamics with high spatial, temporal, and energy resolutions. Building upon transmission electron microscopy (TEM), UEM similarly addresses a wide range of materials science questions via a pulsed electron beam in a pump-probe scheme. Of paramount importance is the capability for UEM to capture dynamics across various excitation phenomena at their native timescales. This includes phenomena such as phonons [1], magnetic domain demagnetization [2], electron spin dynamics [3], and polariton wave dynamics [4]. Furthermore, UEM provides the ability to record transformation and interplay between one collective excitation to another and thus the ability to tune materials systems at the smallest scales. A recent example includes the ability to affect charge density wave phase in TaS2via coherent acoustic phonons [5]. The previous studies use a laser-based approach to UEM where an ultrafast UV laser pulse impinges on the cathode and extracts a packet of photoelectrons. Ideally, the pulse width of the laser-generated photoelectron packet equals the probe-generating laser pulse. However, deleterious space-charge effects as a result of coulomb repulsion from multiple electrons in the probe packet deteriorate spatial resolution and energy spread compared to the continuous beam. Additionally, ultrafast laser repetition rates limited to MHz result in low duty cycles and long experiment times (up to 24 hours) where minimizing sample drift and alignment between the laser system and the microscope become challenging. These drawbacks highlight a critical gap in the current UEM technologies, particularly in achieving stable, high-resolution imaging under varying experimental conditions.
